interactions.label: In fetal circulation, three shunts allow blood to bypass the non-functioning lun

params.question: In fetal circulation, three shunts allow blood to bypass the non-functioning lungs. Which of the following correctly describes the function of the ductus arteriosus?

answers.text: It shunts oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein directly to the inferior vena cava, bypassing the liver

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes the ductus venosus, not the ductus arteriosus. The ductus venosus connects the umbilical vein to the IVC, allowing oxygenated placental blood to reach the heart without passing through the hepatic sinusoids.

answers.text: It diverts blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary circulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The ductus arteriosus shunts blood from the pulmonary artery directly to the descending aorta, bypassing the high-resistance fetal pulmonary vasculature. It closes functionally within hours of birth as pulmonary vascular resistance drops.

answers.text: It allows right-to-left flow of blood between the two atria through a flap valve

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes the foramen ovale — the interatrial communication that allows oxygenated blood returning from the placenta to bypass the right ventricle and reach the systemic circulation directly.

answers.text: It connects the left atrium to the pulmonary veins to increase oxygen delivery to the brain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is anatomically incorrect. The pulmonary veins normally drain into the left atrium. The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta, not the left atrium to the pulmonary veins.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the three fetal shunts: the foramen ovale (right-to-left atrial), the ductus arteriosus (pulmonary artery to aorta), and the ductus venosus (umbilical vein to IVC). Each serves a distinct bypass function in fetal circulation.
Well done. The ductus arteriosus diverts blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta — one of three fetal shunts that bypass the lungs before birth.

interactions.label: A newborn's heart rate remains at 50 bpm after 30 seconds of positive pressure v

params.question: A newborn's heart rate remains at 50 bpm after 30 seconds of positive pressure ventilation with visible chest rise. What is the most appropriate next step?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Adrenaline is indicated only after the heart rate remains <60 bpm despite both effective ventilation AND adequate chest compressions — it is not the immediate next step after PPV alone.

answers.text: Begin chest compressions using the two-thumb encircling method on the lower third of the sternum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Chest compressions are indicated when the heart rate remains <60 bpm despite 30 seconds of effective PPV with confirmed chest rise. The two-thumb encircling method on the lower third of the sternum is the preferred technique.

answers.text: Perform MR SOPA corrective steps to improve ventilation quality

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MR SOPA corrective steps are used when PPV does NOT produce visible chest rise, indicating ineffective ventilation. Here, chest rise is confirmed — ventilation is already effective, and the next escalation is compressions.

answers.text: Discontinue PPV and observe for spontaneous improvement over the next 60 seconds

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: With a heart rate of 50 bpm, discontinuing ventilation and observing would be dangerous. The NRP algorithm mandates immediate escalation to chest compressions when effective PPV has not raised HR above 60 bpm within 30 seconds.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the NRP sequence: effective PPV first (confirm chest rise, correct with MR SOPA if needed), then chest compressions if HR remains <60 bpm after 30 seconds, then adrenaline if compressions also fail.
Excellent. Always confirm effective ventilation (visible chest rise) before starting compressions — compressions on a non-ventilated baby are futile.

interactions.label: A term neonate who suffered birth asphyxia has been stabilised with initial resu

params.question: A term neonate who suffered birth asphyxia has been stabilised with initial resuscitation and supportive NICU care. Which disease-specific intervention is indicated for preventing further neurological injury in hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Phenobarbital is used to treat neonatal seizures but is not the disease-specific neuroprotective intervention for HIE. Its role is symptomatic, not disease-modifying.

answers.text: High-flow oxygen therapy to maximise cerebral oxygenation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The narration specifically warns against hyperoxia — excessive oxygen generates reactive oxygen species that worsen ischaemic brain injury. Oxygen must be titrated by pulse oximetry to avoid both hyperoxia and hypoxia.

Correct. Therapeutic hypothermia is the disease-specific intervention for HIE. It reduces cerebral metabolic demand and attenuates the cascade of secondary neuronal injury following the initial hypoxic-ischaemic insult.
Exchange transfusion is indicated for severe neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia or haemolytic disease — not for HIE. The disease-specific intervention here is therapeutic hypothermia.

overallFeedback.feedback: HIE management rests on three pillars: (1) immediate resuscitation at birth, (2) stabilisation and supportive NICU care, and (3) therapeutic hypothermia — the only disease-specific intervention currently proven to reduce neurological injury.
Well done. The three pillars of HIE management are immediate resuscitation, supportive NICU care, and therapeutic hypothermia as the disease-specific intervention.

interactions.label: A low birth weight neonate whose Ballard score confirms term gestational age but

params.question: A low birth weight neonate whose Ballard score confirms term gestational age but whose weight falls below the 10th centile is classified as preterm.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This neonate is small for gestational age (SGA), not preterm. Prematurity is a gestational age classification (<37 weeks), while SGA is a weight-for-gestational-age classification (below the 10th centile). As the narration emphasises, distinguishing these two mechanisms is the first and most important clinical step — they produce different complications and management priorities.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. A term neonate (GA ≥37 weeks by Ballard scoring) whose weight falls below the 10th centile is small for gestational age (SGA), reflecting intrauterine growth restriction. Prematurity is defined solely by gestational age (<37 completed weeks), not by birth weight.

interactions.label: Following a prolonged vertex delivery, a neonate has bruising over the presentin

params.question: Following a prolonged vertex delivery, a neonate has bruising over the presenting part and a scalp swelling. Which approach best reflects the correct clinical management principle for birth injuries?

answers.text: Reassure the parents that all delivery-related swellings are benign and require no further action

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not all birth injuries are benign — scalp swellings can range from self-limiting caput succedaneum to life-threatening subgaleal haemorrhage. Blanket reassurance without systematic examination is clinically unsafe.

answers.text: Perform a systematic examination to characterise each injury precisely and document findings for medicolegal and parental communication

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Birth injuries demand systematic examination — especially scalp swellings, which require precise characterisation before a diagnosis is assigned. Documentation serves both clinical management and medicolegal/parental communication needs.

answers.text: Order immediate cranial imaging before any clinical assessment of the swelling

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Clinical examination and characterisation must precede imaging decisions. A systematic bedside assessment can determine the type of swelling and guide whether imaging is needed.

answers.text: Delay the neonatal examination until 48 hours after birth when injuries become fully apparent

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While some birth injuries evolve over hours to days, the initial systematic examination must be performed promptly at birth. Delayed assessment risks missing injuries that require urgent intervention.

overallFeedback.feedback: Birth injuries require immediate systematic examination with precise characterisation — particularly scalp swellings after vertex delivery, which must be accurately diagnosed before management decisions. Documentation for medicolegal and parental communication is equally essential.
Well done. Systematic examination, precise characterisation, and thorough documentation are the cornerstones of birth injury assessment.
